translations: Spring breeze arrived first at the North Sea. It swept across the water's surface, stirring up gentle ripples, and lifted the small birds on the cliff into the sky. The giant Peng spread one wing, and the wind passed along its feathers before dispersing.
"Is this enough?" the small bird asked.
"Not enough,"
"What about the gust yesterday?"
"That wasn't enough either."
"Maybe the wind you're waiting for is lost?"
The giant Peng looked towards the north: "It's coming from far away, so it's slow to arrive."

The small bird thought this was just an excuse for waiting, so it flew off elsewhere. The small fish in the water gradually got used to the huge shadow above them. At first, they would wait every day for the giant Peng to take flight, then they started guessing it wouldn't fly, and eventually, they didn't even bother guessing.

The giant Peng didn't explain itself to anyone. Whenever the wind came, it would stretch its wings to feel it. The wind that could lift its feathers but not carry it across the vast sky was only suitable for circling above the North Sea; the wind that rose and fell unpredictably couldn't support a long journey. It had tried a short flight once, gliding over the high cliff before folding its wings and returning, and after that, it only spread its wings when the truly suitable wind arrived.

One day, the warm wind lasted longer than usual. The small birds all said this must be the one. The giant Peng spread its wings and rose to just below the clouds, only to find the wind turned back north when it reached the sea's edge. If it continued to harness the wind, it would only circle the North Sea. So, it turned around in mid-air and landed back on the cliff top, not forcing itself to fly in the wrong direction just because it had taken off.
A small fish asked, "If you can fly, why not fly a bit first?"
The giant Peng said, "I'm going to the south."
"You can fly a bit at a time, and you'll get there eventually."
"But if each segment of the flight is blown off course by the wind, the more I fly, the farther I'll be from my direction."

The small fish didn't believe it. In the North Sea, they never needed to set long-term goals; as long as there was seaweed today and a crevice to hide in tomorrow, they felt their path was already arranged. The giant Peng didn't ask them to understand; it just continued to wait.

The spring breeze passed, and the days grew longer. The sea surface often had warm winds rising, coming and going quickly. The giant Peng wasn't tempted by the temporary lift. It knew that once its wings were fully spread, it wouldn't just leave the cliff top but would also leave the North Sea behind.

The wait wasn't quiet. Small birds came and went, rain fell and stopped, and the sea had winds that blew clouds very low. The giant Peng occasionally spread its wings, and the creatures of the North Sea would look up; it would then calmly fold its wings if it decided the wind wasn't sufficient, not changing its choice because of others' sighs.

The small fish even set up a betting pool: some guessed it would fly the next day, while others guessed it would never fly. The old turtle refused to bet, saying it didn't want to swim up to pay regardless of who won. The giant Peng heard these words and thought the days in the North Sea weren't boring because of the wait.
"Not flying again," the small bird said.
"Not flying recklessly again," the giant Peng corrected.

Time finally reached June. A long cloud appeared on the northern horizon, and then all the small winds on the sea surface stopped. The aquatic creatures hid in the depths, the small birds landed behind the rocks, and even the most argumentative fish closed their mouths.

After a moment, a long, piercing sound came from the distance, a sound that connected the sea and the sky. It wasn't a small wind skimming the waves but a great wind coming from the ends of the earth. The clouds were pushed towards the south, and the water of the North Sea also surged in the same direction.

The giant Peng didn't judge just by the sound. It spread one wing, and the wind continuously supported it, not dispersing behind the cliff; the distant long cloud also kept moving south. All the previous observations, foldings of the wings, and waits finally pointed to the same result.
The giant Peng stood up from its high perch and spread its wings. It wasn't waiting for an auspicious day but for the power that would make this long journey truly happen.
The June wind had finally arrived.

The June wind crossed the North Sea, and there were no more scattered sounds between the sea and the sky. The clouds flowed south, and the waves also bowed south. The giant Peng stood on the high cliff, not chasing the wind, but slowly spreading its wings.

One side of its wing covered the cliff head, and the other side stretched towards the sea surface. The small birds flew far away before they could see clearly that these were no ordinary wings but wings like clouds hanging from the sky, standing between the North Sea and the vast sky.

Aman had already pressed the green bamboo slips under him and protected the old brush with his hands. The waves gently lapped at his feet, as if wanting to sweep the thin bamboo slips into the deep blue North Sea. Aman looked up at the figure that had just transformed into a giant bird — its back scales had turned into layered feathers, like overlapping mountains, and the wingtips still had the wet sheen of seawater.

He wanted to record how far the wingspan reached, and the brush tip trembled slightly on the bamboo slip, first writing "to the sea's edge." However, the sea wind suddenly picked up, lifting the edge of the slip, and the brush tip wavered, accidentally changing "sea" to "sky." Aman frowned, muttering, "This wind is even helping me change my words."

He put the brush back on the slip, deciding to write again, this time focusing on the wing that seemed like a cloud hanging from the sky, wanting to write "to the edge of the sky." Just as the brush stroke was made, the giant Peng's chest fin suddenly trembled, stirring up a wave, and a water droplet splashed onto the left corner of the bamboo slip. The droplet, like a mischievous sprite, slid down along the brush stroke, changing the last part of the "sky" character into a small "mouth" character. Aman looked up to see a few small fish curiously watching this "writing show" from a distance.
